title: Who owns the past?
text: Walk through the British Museum and you pass objects collected under conditions that no modern curator would {{1}}: the Parthenon sculptures, removed by an ambassador; the Benin bronzes, taken by a punitive expedition; the Rosetta Stone, {{2}} from Egypt by an occupying army. For two centuries the answer to demands for return never really {{3}}: once acquired, objects belonged to the museum, and museums belonged to everyone. That settlement is {{4}}. The Benin bronzes are now scattered across more than a hundred collections, and German and Nigerian institutions have {{5}} agreements transferring ownership outright; Ethiopia has recovered a crown; Manchester Museum has simply {{6}} objects to Aboriginal custodians. The debate has moved from whether to how: conditions of conservation, who pays, and what a museum is for once its galleries {{7}} of trophy pieces. Defenders of the status quo argue that universal museums let humanity see itself in one place, and that returns can {{8}} fragile states to demand every object back. Critics reply that universal too often meant imperial, and that the objects' own countries never had a say.

gaps.explanation: 'conditions no modern curator would defend' — justify; defer = postpone out of respect, defy = openly refuse to obey.
'removed from Egypt by an occupying army' — taken away; remand = hold in custody, remunerate = pay.
'never really varied' — always stayed the same; verify = confirm as true, violate = break a rule.
'that settlement is crumbling' — disintegrating; rumble = make a deep noise, fumble = handle clumsily.
'have signed agreements' — put their names to them; sight = spot visually, cite = quote, side takes 'with'.
'has simply handed objects to Aboriginal custodians' — given them over; hoard = store up secretly, hinder = obstruct.
'once its galleries empty of trophy pieces' — 'empty' works as a verb here: the galleries lose their contents; exonerate = clear of blame.
'returns can embolden fragile states to demand every object back' — make them confident enough to; enfeeble = weaken.
